application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A mixed-criticality system integrates subsystems with different criticality levels on the shared hardware platform, significantly improving resource utilization and becoming an important research topic for embedded systems. However, most existing works on scheduling strategies for mixed-criticality systems are based on independent task sets. This paper designs a scheduling strategy considering task data dependencies and real-time operating system constraints. In addition, this paper saves energy costs by using DVFS to adjust task execution frequency dynamically. Specifically, a multiple DAG task scheduling strategy is designed for the heterogeneous platform, exploring idle time through DVFS to optimize system energy cost in low-criticality mode with the consideration of ensuring task schedulability while fully utilizing multiprocessing to enhance system performance in the highcriticality mode. Experimental results show that our method can guarantee the quality of service and optimize the system energy cost compared with the existing methods.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Complex Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) often need to integrate applications with different criticality levels, which can be effectively addressed by Mixed-Criticality Systems (MCS). MCS integrates multiple subsystems with varying levels of criticality in applications such as aircraft and automotive systems [1]. The concept of MCS was first proposed by [2] and has drawn much attention. The dual-criticality systems are studied in [3]- [14], where the tasks with high-criticality levels and low-criticality levels share the same execution platform. To ensure that the high-criticality tasks do not miss their deadlines, the system sacrifices executing the low-criticality tasks, which pessimistically reduces system QoS (Quality of Service). The Adaptive Mixed Criticality (AMC) model is proposed for sporadic task sets with fixed priority levels on the single processor [3]. When the high-criticality task exceeds its low-criticality WCET (Worst Case Execution Time) estimate, the execution of all low-criticality tasks will be stopped immediately, and the criticality level of the system is triggered to switch from lowcriticality level mode (LO-mode) to high-criticality level mode (HI-mode). However, AMC is pessimistic and unacceptable in many practical systems. In system HI-mode, the QoS level should be guaranteed [4]. The Elastic Mixed Criticality (EMC) task model improves system QoS level, as low-criticality tasks have variable periods [5]. When the system changes the execution mode, the release period of low-criticality tasks is gradually extended instead of pessimistic stopping execution. The Flexible Mixed Criticality (FMC) model is proposed [6], where the QoS level is gradually reduced along with the number of the overruns of high-criticality tasks, and the mode-switches of high-criticality tasks are independent, only the task that exceeds the low-criticality WCET is switched to the high-criticality WCET instead of all the high-criticality tasks. In addition, some works explore the Imprecise Mixed Criticality (IMC) model, e.g., [7], where the execution time of low-criticality tasks is reduced to a certain extent in the system's high-criticality mode.

The above studies focus on the independent mixed-criticality task model, ignoring the correlation and parallelism between tasks. However, in many practical applications, tasks have data dependencies, and a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) can describe the relationship between tasks. The DAG task graph considers the correlation constraint of tasks and the communication relationship between tasks. Federated scheduling on mixed-criticality DAG tasks in a multiprocessor environment is considered in [8], where the high utilization tasks are assigned to the target processors and other tasks are transferred to the remaining processors. For multiple DAGs, a task scheduling algorithm is proposed in [9] to reduce task makespan, and a task scheduling algorithm is designed in [10] to optimize DMR (deadline missed ratios).

Optimizing energy cost in mixed-criticality systems is also important with the increase in computing demands and embedded systems often deployed in energy-constrained environments. DVFS technology can dynamically adjust the system's operation rate, optimizing its energy cost. In [11], DVFS is applied for mixed-criticality systems and combined with the EDF-VD [3] (Earliest Deadline First with Virtual Deadlines) scheduling, which is modeled as a convex programming problem for energy minimization. On this basis, the idle time slots are effectively explored in the reserved time (i.e., the gap between high-criticality WCET and low-criticality WCET) of high-criticality tasks to reduce energy consumption [12]. In [13], an energy-aware IMC scheduling algorithm is designed for the IMC task set. Based on FMC, an energy-efficient scheduling method combined with the service level guarantee mechanism is proposed in [14]. However, the above studies are based on the mixed-criticality independent task model and do not consider task dependency, which is more general and realistic. Compared with the existing works, this paper addresses the energy minimization problem for scheduling multiple mixedcriticality DAG tasks with DVFS.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model and formulates the task scheduling problem. Section III introduces the proposed mixed-criticality task scheduling algorithm. Section IV shows and analyzes the simulation results. Section V concludes this paper.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM FORMULATION
1) Platform Model:
div.p: We consider the heterogeneous multicore platform with N processors P = {p 1 , . . . , p N }. The power consumption of a processor consists of static power P s , dynamic power P d , and speed-independent power P ind . P s is generated by a subthreshold leakage current that persists when the system is turned on, and P s is reduced to 0 when the system is turned off. P d = C ef f f 2 is caused by the circuit switching activity and is related to the processor operating frequency, where C ef f represents the effective switching capacitance, and f is the processor operating frequency. P ind is due to the I/O operations and memory activity. Therefore, the power consumption of the processor can be given by P (f ) = P s + h(P ind + P d ) = P s +h(P ind +C ef f f 2 ). If the system is active, h = 1; otherwise, h = 0. The above equation shows that the processor power is proportional to the processor frequency. We adopt the energy consumption model from [15], focusing on the active power and ignoring the static power, i.e., P s = 0.

2) Mixed-criticality Task Model: We consider an independent mixed-criticality application set A = {A 1 , . . . , A G }, where each application A m with multiple dependent tasks is described by a DAG A m (V m , E m ). V m represents the task set, while E m represents the edge set (task dependency) between the tasks. We model application A m ∈ A by a tuple

C m (HI) represents the WCET matrix of tasks in application A m when the system is in the HI-mode. C k,i,m (LO) and C k,i,m (HI) represent the WCET of task τ i in application V m , when τ i is assigned to processor p k and the system is working on the LO-mode and HImode, respectively. Note that we only consider the heterogeneity among the computation, i.e., the links between the processors are assumed to have the same communication rate. T m and D m represent the period and the relative deadline of application A m , respectively. Without loss of generality, we adopt the concept of the implicit deadline [8], where the relative deadline of a task is equal to its period, i.e., D m = T m . Moreover, the task sets of low-criticality and high-criticality are defined as Γ LO = {τ i ∈ V m |χ m = LO} and Γ HI = {τ i ∈ V m |χ m = HI}, respectively. Usually, the mixed-criticality system is a real-time system that runs multiple applications with different criticality levels simultaneously. Thus, the corresponding system criticality level set is χ s ∈ {LO, HI}. Each application is assigned a criticality level, while all tasks in an application have the same criticality.

div.head: III. HEURISTIC EFFICIENT SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section, we propose an energy-efficient scheduling method for mixed-criticality tasks consisting of design-time and run-time phases. The structure of our method is shown in Fig. 1. In the design-time phase, we get the application set and its execution and communication parameters at the software level, as well as the parameters of heterogeneous processors at the hardware level, e.g., the optional frequencies. On this basis, we carry out a two-step mixed-criticality system static scheduling method, which involves task allocation and scheduling in the first step, followed by efficient frequency selection in the second step. The proposed method is summarized in Algorithms 1 and 2, to minimize the system LO-mode energy consumption. Then, in the run-time phase, we optimize the system QoS by designing the mode-switching strategy, summarized in Algorithm 3.

Let Γ denote the set of tasks in the application set A, i.e., Γ = m∈G V m , and note that the total number of tasks is M = m∈G |V m |. In Algorithm 1, for each task τ i in the system task set Γ, we calculate each task's rank u value and sort these tasks, where the time complexity is O(MlogM) [10], and then allocate each task τ i to a processor p k ∈ P. Since the system has N processors, the time complexity is O(MN). 2) Efficient Frequency Selection: This section focuses on the energy-saving problem during the system LO-mode period since the mixed-criticality systems work most of the time on this mode [13]. We explore the idle time slots through the DVFS technology under time constraints. For each low and high-criticality task τ i , we define LST (τ i ) and LF T (τ i ) as the Latest Start Time and Latest Finish Time of τ i , respectively. In the mixed-criticality systems, the values of LF T (τ i ) for different criticality level tasks are different. Let D i denote the relative deadline of task τ i in system LO-mode, i.e., τ i must complete its execution before time D i . As shown in Fig. 2(a), for the low-criticality task τ i , since τ i has the same WCET in both system LO-mode and HI-mode, LF T (τ i ) is equal to the relative deadline D i , i.e., LF T (τ i ) = D i . If τ i is an exit task, i.e., it has no successors, the relative deadline D i of τ i is the same as the deadline D m of DAG A m (τ i ∈ V m ); otherwise, D i is bounded by the task allocation result from the previous step and the successors of τ i , and thus, we need to calculate the value of LF T (τ i ) from the exit task. If task τ i is allocated to processor p k , we can get the following task of τ i on the same processor p k , e.g., τ j , and thus, LF T (τ i ) must be no more than LST (τ j ), i.e., LF T (τ i ) ≤ LST (τ j ). Moreover, the communication time w i,j,m between τ i and its successor should be taken into account. Therefore, we set D i = min τj ∈succ(τi) {LST (τ j ) -w i,j,m }, and LST (τ i ) = LF T (τ i ) -δ i , where δ i is the actual executable time of task τ i on processor p k with (v l , f l ) frequency level in system χ smode, i.e., δ i = Ck,i,m(χ s )fk,max fk,l . However, suppose we use the same method as the lowcriticality tasks to calculate the relative deadline D i for the high-criticality task τ i . In that case, the real-time constraint can not be satisfied when the system mode switch occurs, as shown in Fig. 2(b). This is because the WCEC (Worst Case Execution Cycles) of high-criticality tasks in system HImode is larger than that in system LO-mode by f k,max × [C k,i,m (HI) -C k,i,m (LO)], i.e., the high-criticality task needs to take additional execution cycles into account after the system mode switches to HI-mode. Therefore, when calculating the relative deadline D i for the high-criticality task τ i in the system LO-mode, we need to reserve a time budget to deal with the occurrence of mode switching. If the processor executes at the energy-saving frequency in LO-mode, it switches to the maximum frequency f max in HI-mode by DVFS, and executes the high-criticality task in C k,i,m (HI) (Lines 2-3). For the sake of presentation, the high-criticality task that overruns and triggers the system mode transition is denoted as τ ov . If τ ov ∈ V m , the DAG of V m is denoted as A ov (Lines 5-6). Since all the tasks in V m have finished their executions, the system no longer needs the HI-mode to maintain the execution demand of the high-criticality task. Note that the exit task is the latest one in the DAG. When task τ exit ∈ V m completes its execution, the system falls back to the low-criticality mode (Lines 15-17).

During the system HI-mode, we aim to ensure the system QoS, i.e., QoS(χ s = HI). Note that the earliest execution time of a task in the DAG is affected by the communication time between its predecessors and itself. A task cannot execute even if the processor is idle due to the data dependency between this task and its predecessor. For example, since the highcriticality tasks in DAG of application A 1 (χ 1 = HI) have data dependencies (Fig. 4(a)), the execution of task τ 3 on processor p 2 needs to wait for the data of its predecessor τ 1 on another processor p 1 with communication time w 1,3,1 , resulting in the generation of idle time slot Δ 1 (Fig. 4(b)). Similarly, the execution of τ 3 on p 2 needs to transfer data to its successor τ 5 on p 1 , and the communication time required to transfer data is w 3,5,1 , leading to the idle time slot Δ 2 . The idle time slots can be used to execute low-criticality tasks without data dependencies to improve the system QoS. To reduce the task time on the processor, the low-criticality tasks are executed with the maximum frequency f k,max (Line 4).

Executing a low-criticality task in the idle time slot should not affect the execution of a high-criticality task. If a highcriticality task starts to execute during a low-criticality task, we immediately discard the low-criticality task that is executing. To obtain the actual execution time of low-criticality tasks, we need to calculate the estimated finish time of each lowcriticality task, i.e., t ef i,m = t s i,m + C k,i,m (HI). This task can continue to execute until one of the high-criticality tasks on the same processor is ready. Thus, the preempt time of task τ i is t P T i,m = min{LST (τ j )}, ∀τ j ∈ Γ HI Γ k , where τ j ∈ Γ HI Γ k represents τ j is a high-criticality task and is allocated on the same processor p k as task τ i . Then, we calculate t ef i,m through t P T i,m (Line 9). As shown in Fig. 4(c), if t ef i,m > t P T i,m , i.e., the execution time of a low-criticality task reaches the latest start time of a high-criticality task (i.e., LST (τ 5 )), the low-criticality task is preempted, and its execution time will be released to the high-criticality task (Lines 10-11); else, the lowcriticality task can be completed as the expected estimate, i.e., t f i,m = t ef i,m (Line 13), as shown in Fig. 4(d).

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENT RESULTS
div.p: For the experimental setup, the processor parameters (e.g., v l , f l , and P l ) are adopted from [18], and the task parameters (e.g., C m and W m ) are adopted from [19]. We generate random DAGs for our method. Fig. 5 compares the energy consumption under system LO-mode solving by the Gurobi solver (OPT) and the proposed heuristic algorithm (HEU). Fig. 5(a) compares the energy consumption under different utilization rates, and the results show that the system energy consumption increases with the system utilization rate. This is because the system utilization rate reflects the ratio of task execution time to task period, i.e., U (χ s ) = τi∈Γ Ci(χ s ) Ti . When the system utilization rate increases, the relaxation time of each task is shortened. Thus, the optimization frequency of the task is higher, leading to an increase in system energy cost. Fig. 5(b) shows that with the task number M increasing, e.g., from 10 to 60, the energy cost of OPT and HEU both increase. Although the energy consumption of the proposed HEU is 9.1% higher than that of OPT, the computation time of OPT grows exponentially with the number of tasks, and the computation time of HEU is usually within 1 s, which is negligible compared with OPT. Note that the mode transition time occurs at any time, which is hard to predict in advance. The optimal solution can only be obtained under the premise that the mode transition time is determined. The optimal solution found in Fig. 5 can only be used as a reference for the evaluation of the performance of our heuristic algorithm. During the simulations, we consider the system mode switching is triggered at any time. Fig. 6 compares the system energy cost with and without Algorithm 2 (i.e., with and without DVFS). Since Algorithm 2 is mainly used to optimize the system energy cost, the result shows that we achieve energyefficient scheduling by using Algorithm 2 under different system utilization rates and different task numbers. Fig. 6(a) shows that the proposed method has better energy-saving performance when the system utilization rate is low. This is because the lower the system utilization rate, the more idle time the processors have. The system energy cost can be reduced using idle time to optimize the task execution frequency. Fig. 6(b) shows that our method achieved an average energy savings of 13.65% as task number M increases from 10 to 60. Fig. 7(a) evaluates the influence of task DAG on energysaving performance. We set the total task number M = 100 and consider multiple applications. In application A m , the task set V m can be modeled by a task DAG with V = |V m | nodes, where we change V ∈ {5, 10, 20}, and the larger the value of V , the fewer applications and more tasks are in one application. In addition, the energy-saving percent is defined as the gap with and without Algorithm 2. The results show that when the system utilization rate is within [0.3, 0.6] and we set V = 20, the system has a better energy-saving performance. This is because, when the total task number M is fixed, the larger V , the more edges in one DAG, leading to a more complex correlation between the tasks, i.e., more data dependencies among the tasks. When these tasks are mapped on the processors, more idle time on the processor due to data transfer, which can be used for frequency optimization, resulting in a higher energysaving. Fig. 7(b) shows the impact of high-criticality DAG tasks proportion in all tasks on energy-saving performance. To describe the high-criticality DAG tasks proportion, we introduce a parameter = m∈G,χm =HI |Vm| m∈G,χm=LO∪HI |Vm| . The results show that the energy cost increases as the parameter increases. This is because, with the proportion of high-criticality DAG tasks increasing, more time slots need to be reserved to ensure the completion of high-criticality tasks on time, resulting in fewer time slots that can be used for energy saving.

Fig. 8 compares the energy cost and system QoS under different system utilization rates by using the proposed mixedcriticality task model with preemption (i.e., DPMC), FMC model [14], and IMC model [13]. The results show that DPMC has better energy-saving performance, when the system utilization rate is lower than 0.9. In addition, DPMC can achieve a higher system QoS than FMC and IMC. This is because we fully utilize the time slots between high-criticality tasks to execute low-criticality tasks, improving the system QoS.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposes an energy-efficient mixed-criticality task scheduling algorithm for the heterogeneous multicore platform to optimize the energy cost of mixed-criticality systems in lowcriticality mode and system QoS in high-criticality mode. To optimize the energy and QoS objectives under task dependency and real-time response constraints, task allocation and scheduling, as well as frequency selection, are jointly considered. Considering random system mode transition time, we design a two-step heuristic method to decompose the original problem to reduce computation time. The simulation results show that our mixed-criticality task scheduling method can optimize the system energy cost under multiple constraints and outperform other methods regarding QoS guarantee.
